\section{External Evaluation in Detail}
\label{app:external}
%% ============================================================================

\paragraph{Protocol.} Table~\ref{tab:ext-data} lists the data, and Figure~\ref{fig:external}
shows the main results for the GPT-6 miner.
Apps.~\ref{app:ext-logical}--\ref{app:asap} follow the four properties of
\S\ref{sec:exp-external}, and App.~\ref{app:ext-further} collects further analyses: the sign of
each relation at every truth assignment, ContraDoc at the verdict world, and how well the miner
recovers the relations annotated in QT30 and GDTB. The settings are:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.2em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=2pt]
\item the graph-level miner with GPT-6 and with gpt-oss-120b, two arms ($k=5$, the taxonomy of Table~\ref{tab:couplings}, the gateway's response
  cache bypassed);
\item $\LCS$ and $\Lambda$ with flat priors, $\Lambda$ exact by variable elimination on each
  connected component;
\item invariance within $\tau=0.01$;
\item two-sided exact sign tests and 95\% bootstrap intervals over the natural group (family,
  source document or nodeset).
\end{itemize}
The baselines are those of \S\ref{sec:exp-baselines} that read a single text: DiscoScore RC and
LC, the entity graph and G-Eval with GPT-6, averaged over three runs (five for the essays of App.~\ref{app:asap}, and five in
\S\ref{sec:exp-baselines}, for the larger corpora). To measure the miner's noise floor,
ContraDoc's clean documents were mined a second time with fresh samples, as the LoCoBench records
already allow.
\paragraph{The sign test.} Several analyses compare paired scores, such as a document before
and after a contradiction is inserted, and predict the direction of the change. For each pair we
record only whether the score fell, rose or tied, and drop the ties. If the edit had no systematic
effect, a fall and a rise would be equally likely, so among the $n$ untied pairs the number of falls
would follow a $\mathrm{Binomial}(n,\frac12)$ distribution. The $p$-value is the probability, under
that null, of a split at least as lopsided as the one observed. It is \emph{two-sided}: it counts
lopsidedness in either direction, which is the more conservative choice for a directional
prediction (roughly doubling $p$). The test uses only the
direction of each change, not its size, so it needs no assumption about how the changes are
distributed, which matters because changes in $\LCS$ range from tiny to several nats. For example,
inserting a contradiction into a ContraDoc document lowers $\LCS$ on \extCdAssertDecGpt{} pairs and
raises it on \extCdAssertIncGpt{} (Table~\ref{tab:ext-contradoc}); under the null, a split this
uneven has probability below $\extCdAssertPGpt$. Tables report $p$ as such an upper bound, a power
of ten, when it is very small. A small $p$ says that the direction of the effect is not a sampling
accident. It says nothing about the effect's size, which the split itself conveys, and it does not
cover systematic errors such as a biased miner, which the design and the Limitations address.

%% ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Related to, but Not a Proxy for, Discourse Coherence}
\label{app:ext-logical}

\paragraph{SummEval.} $\LCS$ with every claim true correlates with the expert ratings as follows:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.2em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=2pt]
\item coherence, $\extSeRhoCohGpt$ {\scriptsize[\extSeRhoCohGptLo,\,\extSeRhoCohGptHi]};
\item consistency, $\extSeRhoConsistencyGpt$;
\item fluency, $\extSeRhoFluencyGpt$;
\item relevance, $\extSeRhoRelevanceGpt$.
\end{itemize}
SummEval's ``consistency'' is faithfulness to the source article, which the score does not
measure. The G-Eval judge correlates with the same coherence ratings at
$\rho=\extSeJudgeRhoCoh$, as a discourse-coherence measure should. With gpt-oss-120b, the
correlation with coherence is $\extSeRhoCohOss$
{\scriptsize[\extSeRhoCohOssLo,\,\extSeRhoCohOssHi]}.

\paragraph{Summaries with relations.} \extSeEmptyGpt\% of the summaries, about three sentences
long, have no factor relation at all and score exactly $\frac12$, which dilutes any correlation.
On the \extSeNonEmptyNGpt{} that have one, the correlation with rated coherence is
$\extSeNonEmptyRhoCohGpt$ {\scriptsize[\extSeNonEmptyRhoCohGptLo,\,\extSeNonEmptyRhoCohGptHi]}
(G-Eval: $\extSeNonEmptyJudgeRhoCohGpt$). The graphs are almost conflict-free: of their
\extSeRelAllGpt{} relations, \extSeRelInferenceGpt{} are inferences, \extSeRelRestatementGpt{}
restatements and \extSeRelConflictGpt{} conflicts. The two kinds of support part ways:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.2em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=2pt]
\item the number of restatements correlates with rated coherence at
  $\extSeCountRestateRhoCohGpt$ {\scriptsize[\extSeCountRestateRhoCohGptLo,\,\extSeCountRestateRhoCohGptHi]},
  and the number of inferences at $\extSeCountInfRhoCohGpt$
  {\scriptsize[\extSeCountInfRhoCohGptLo,\,\extSeCountInfRhoCohGptHi]};
\item on the \extSeInfOnlyNGpt{} summaries whose graph has inferences but no restatement, $\LCS$
  correlates with rated coherence at $\extSeInfOnlyRhoCohGpt$
  {\scriptsize[\extSeInfOnlyRhoCohGptLo,\,\extSeInfOnlyRhoCohGptHi]}, and on the
  \extSeRestateNGpt{} with a restatement at $\extSeRestateRhoCohGpt$
  {\scriptsize[\extSeRestateRhoCohGptLo,\,\extSeRestateRhoCohGptHi]}.
\end{itemize}
A restatement of an asserted claim is logically consistent, so the score counts it as a support,
while raters penalize the redundancy it signals; the summarizers that repeat themselves most are
rated least coherent. With gpt-oss-120b the pattern is the same: $\extSeNonEmptyRhoCohOss$ on the
\extSeNonEmptyNOss{} summaries with a relation, $\extSeCountRestateRhoCohOss$ for the number of
restatements and $\extSeInfOnlyRhoCohOss$ on inference-only graphs.

\paragraph{Ablation and signed sum (exploratory).} Dropping every restatement factor and keeping
the rest of each graph, $\LCS$ correlates with rated coherence at $\extSeNoRestateRhoCohGpt$ over
all summaries and at $\extSeNoRestateNonEmptyRhoCohGpt$
{\scriptsize[\extSeNoRestateNonEmptyRhoCohGptLo,\,\extSeNoRestateNonEmptyRhoCohGptHi]} over those with
a relation (gpt-oss-120b: $\extSeNoRestateRhoCohOss$ and $\extSeNoRestateNonEmptyRhoCohOss$). The
inferences that remain therefore make a summary both more logically and more discursively
coherent, and it is the restatements that pull the two apart. The signed weight sum is
uncorrelated with rated coherence ($\extSeWsumRhoCohGpt$; $\extSeWsumNonEmptyRhoCohGpt$ on the
summaries with a relation). A score that counts a restatement as support rewards repetition, which
raters penalize; capping repeated support is one remedy, which we leave to future work.

\subsection{Detected Conflicts Lower the Score}
\label{app:ext-contra}

With every claim true, a contradiction is violated, so adding one lowers $\Lambda$
(Lemma~\ref{lem:edit}). In ContraDoc and ChatProtect the added sentence is also a new claim, and a
claim that no relation touches already moves $\LCS$ slightly by changing $u_0$
(App.~\ref{app:lcs-lambda}), so the fall is a prediction about the data rather than an instance of
Theorem~\ref{thm:mono}, which holds the claim set fixed.

\paragraph{ContraDoc insertion pairs.} With every claim true, inserting the contradicting
sentence lowers $\LCS$ on \extCdAssertDecGpt{} and raises it on \extCdAssertIncGpt{} of the
\extCdPairs{} pairs ($p<\extCdAssertPGpt$), and where the miner finds the contradiction it falls
on \extCdAssertEdgeDecGpt{} of \extCdAssertEdgeNGpt{} (Table~\ref{tab:ext-contradoc}). Three further
findings need comment:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.2em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=2pt]
\item \textbf{The committee confirms the verdict reading.} It judged \extCdSpotContradicted{} of
  the \extCdPairs{} inserted sentences contradicted by the rest of their document.
\item \textbf{DiscoScore RC and LC rise when a contradiction is inserted.} This is presumably
  because the inserted sentence repeats the nouns of the sentence it contradicts, which these
  scores reward as cohesion.
\item \textbf{The judge falls too.} G-Eval falls on \extCdJudgeDec{} pairs and never rises, so
  contradiction detection alone does not separate $\LCS$ from a judge.
\end{itemize}
\paragraph{ChatProtect.} With every claim true, adding the second sentence lowers $\LCS$ on \extCpAssertDecGpt{} and raises it on
\extCpAssertIncGpt{} of \extCpAssertNGpt{} contradictory pairs ($p<\extCpAssertPGpt$). Split by whether
the contradiction was found:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.2em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=2pt]
\item where it was found, $\LCS$ falls on \extCpFoundFallGpt{} pairs and rises on
  \extCpFoundRiseGpt;
\item where it was not, it falls on \extCpNotFoundFallGpt{} and rises on \extCpNotFoundRiseGpt.
\end{itemize}
Every rise is a pair whose contradiction the miner missed; the score itself never moves the wrong
way.

With gpt-oss-120b, $\LCS$ falls on all \extCpFoundFallOss{} pairs where the miner finds the
contradiction, but it finds so few (below) that over all pairs falls and
rises are even (\extCpAssertDecOss{} and \extCpAssertIncOss; $p=\extCpAssertPOss$).

\paragraph{Control, ties and effect sizes.} On ChatProtect's \extCpCtlNGpt{} pairs annotated as not
contradictory, adding the second sentence raises $\LCS$ on \extCpCtlIncGpt{}, lowers it on
\extCpCtlDecGpt{} and leaves it unchanged on \extCpCtlTieGpt{} (median change
$\extCpEffCtlMedianGpt$): a consistent sentence earns supports. On the \extCpAssertNGpt{}
contradictory pairs, \extCpAssertTieGpt{} ties come from prefixes whose graph is unchanged. The
median change is $\extCpEffFoundMedianGpt$ where the contradiction is found
($\extCdEffFoundMedianGpt$ on ContraDoc) and $\extCpEffNotFoundMedianGpt$ where it is missed
($\extCdEffNotFoundMedianGpt$ on ContraDoc, where the missed pairs fall \extCdAssertNotFoundDecGpt{}
times and rise \extCdAssertNotFoundIncGpt{}, $p=\extCdAssertNotFoundPGpt$). The signed weight sum
over the same graphs falls on \extCdWsumDecGpt{} and rises on \extCdWsumIncGpt{} ContraDoc pairs
(\extCdWsumEdgeDecGpt{} and \extCdWsumEdgeIncGpt{} where the contradiction is found), and on
\extCpWsumDecGpt{} and \extCpWsumIncGpt{} ChatProtect pairs. Paired (exact McNemar tests on falls), the
two differ on ContraDoc only where the contradiction is found (\extCdMcFoundOnlyLcsGpt{} pairs where
only $\LCS$ falls against \extCdMcFoundOnlySumGpt{}, $p=\extCdMcFoundPGpt$; over all pairs
\extCdMcAllOnlyLcsGpt{} against \extCdMcAllOnlySumGpt, $p=\extCdMcAllPGpt$). On ChatProtect $\LCS$ falls
alone on \extCpMcAllOnlyLcsGpt{} pairs and the sum on \extCpMcAllOnlySumGpt{} ($p<\extCpMcAllPGpt$), but
\extCpMcNotFoundOnlyLcsGpt{} of those are pairs with no detected contradiction, and on the consistent
control $\LCS$ falls alone at the same rate (\extCpMcCtlOnlyLcsGpt{} of \extCpCtlNGpt{} pairs, against
\extCpMcCtlOnlySumGpt{} for the sum; $p=\extCpMcCtlPGpt$). The difference is therefore not sensitivity
to contradictions: the added sentence is also a new claim, which moves $\LCS$ slightly through
$u_0$ (App.~\ref{app:lcs-lambda}) and leaves the sum unchanged.


\paragraph{Recall and false alarms.} On ContraDoc, the GPT-6 arm finds the contradiction in \extCdRecallGpt\% of the 449
contradicted documents (gpt-oss-120b: \extCdRecallOss\%):
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.2em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=2pt]
\item by edit: \extCdRecallInsertGpt\% of insertions and \extCdRecallReplaceGpt\% of
  replacements;
\item by scope: \extCdRecallGlobalGpt\% global
  {\scriptsize[\extCdRecallGlobalGptLo,\,\extCdRecallGlobalGptHi]}, \extCdRecallLocalGpt\% local
  {\scriptsize[\extCdRecallLocalGptLo,\,\extCdRecallLocalGptHi]} and \extCdRecallIntraGpt\%
  within a sentence {\scriptsize[\extCdRecallIntraGptLo,\,\extCdRecallIntraGptHi]};
\item by document type: \extCdRecallNewsGpt\% news, \extCdRecallStoryGpt\% stories and
  \extCdRecallWikiGpt\% Wikipedia.
\end{itemize}
Recall is lowest within a sentence, because a contradiction there is internal to a single claim at sentence granularity, so no
relation between two claims can find it; finer claims, as from an atomizer, could. A replacement
removes the sentence the new one would contradict, which leaves the miner less to link to. On the
442 clean documents, \extCdFpGpt\% of graphs contain at least one contradiction, the false-alarm
rate against which recall should be read; per claim pair, the rate is $\extCdFpPairGpt$
(gpt-oss-120b: \extCdFpOss\% of graphs, $\extCdFpPairOss$ per pair).

On ChatProtect, the GPT-6 arm finds the contradiction in \extCpConfStrongGpt\% of the pairs annotated as
contradictory and in \extCpConfNoneGpt\% of the others: low recall, no false alarms.
gpt-oss-120b finds it in \extCpConfStrongOss\% and \extCpConfNoneOss\% of the two groups.

\subsection{Order}
\label{app:ext-order}

\centering\footnotesize

\begin{tabular}{@{}lccc@{}}
\toprule
& LoCoBench & LoCoBench & ContraDoc \\
& permuted & sent.\ shuffled & permuted \\
\midrule
gold $\LCS$ & 100 & 100 & -- \\
$\LCS$, GPT-6 arm & \extLocoPermInvGpt & \extLocoSentInvGpt & \extCdPermInvGpt \\
\quad re-mined & \extLocoNoiseInvGpt & & \extCdNoiseInvGpt \\
$\LCS$, gpt-oss arm & \extLocoPermInvOss & \extLocoSentInvOss & \extCdPermInvOss \\
\quad re-mined & \extLocoNoiseInvOss & & \extCdNoiseInvOss \\
\midrule
DiscoScore RC$^\dagger$ & \extLocoPermInvRc & \extLocoSentInvRc & \extCdPermInvRc \\
DiscoScore LC$^\dagger$ & \extLocoPermInvLc & \extLocoSentInvLc & \extCdPermInvLc \\
entity graph & \extLocoPermInvEntity & \extLocoSentInvEntity & \extCdPermInvEntity \\
G-Eval, GPT-6 & \extLocoPermInvJudge & \extLocoSentInvJudge & \extCdPermInvJudge \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{\textbf{Order.} Share (\%) of cases a score keeps within $\tau$ on its own scale.
$^\dagger$Order-free by definition: they count noun repetitions regardless of sentence order;
the ContraDoc changes presumably come from sentence segmentation. ``Re-mined'': the share an unchanged text keeps when
it is mined again, the ceiling the mined rows can reach.}
\label{tab:ext-order}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Order.} Gold-graph $\LCS$ is identical across every permutation, as it must be: the
claims and relations do not change. With the GPT-6 arm, the mined score moves about as much as
re-mining moves it (Table~\ref{tab:ext-order}):
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.2em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=2pt]
\item on LoCoBench, a mean absolute change of \extLocoPermMeanGpt{} under permutation; beyond
  $\tau$ it falls on \extLocoPermDownTolGpt{} and rises on \extLocoPermUpTolGpt{} of
  \extLocoPermNGpt{} permutations;
\item on ContraDoc, a mean change of \extCdPermMeanGpt{} under permutation against
  \extCdNoiseMeanGpt{} under re-mining.
\end{itemize}
gpt-oss-120b is noisier, and permutation moves its score more than re-mining does: a mean change
of \extCdPermMeanOss{} against \extCdNoiseMeanOss{} on ContraDoc. For that miner, part of the
movement comes from the order in which it reads the text.
The noise grows with document length (median 39 claims on ContraDoc against 14 on LoCoBench),
because five sampled graphs over many claims agree less often. More samples per document would
lower it. Sentence shuffles move the mined score slightly more (\extLocoSentInvGpt\% within
$\tau$), as expected: they break the anaphora the miner reads. The G-Eval judge falls on
\extLocoPermDecJudge\% of LoCoBench permutations, \extLocoSentDecJudge\% of sentence shuffles
and \extCdPermDecJudge\% of ContraDoc permutations.


The entity graph is the most stable score in Table~\ref{tab:ext-order} because it barely reacts to
anything: it scores only nouns shared by nearby sentences, and on LoCoBench it rises on none of the
declared increases (Figure~\ref{fig:ladders}).

\paragraph{Equivalence and drift.} We test whether permutation moves $\LCS$ no more than
re-mining does by two one-sided tests at $\alpha=0.05$ with margin $\tau$ on the difference in mean
absolute change, using a 90\% group-bootstrap interval. On LoCoBench the difference is
$\extLocoEqDiffGpt$ with interval [\extLocoEqLoGpt, \extLocoEqHiGpt]; on ContraDoc it is
$\extCdEqDiffGpt$ with [\extCdEqLoGpt, \extCdEqHiGpt]. Neither interval lies inside $(-\tau,\tau)$,
so equivalence is not established, narrowly on LoCoBench. The direction of the changes beyond
$\tau$ matters as well. On LoCoBench, re-mining is balanced (\extLocoEqNoiseUpGpt{} rises,
\extLocoEqNoiseDownGpt{} falls, $p=\extLocoEqNoisePGpt$), and permutation leans down
(\extLocoEqPermUpGpt{} and \extLocoEqPermDownGpt, $p=\extLocoEqPermPGpt$). On ContraDoc both lean
up: permutation \extCdEqPermUpGpt{} against \extCdEqPermDownGpt{} ($p=\extCdEqPermPGpt$), and
re-mining \extCdEqNoiseUpGpt{} against \extCdEqNoiseDownGpt{} ($p=\extCdEqNoisePGpt$), although the
re-run used the same configuration about an hour after the original.

\paragraph{Matched design.} To settle the ContraDoc comparison, each of the 150 originals and its
two permutations was mined twice more with GPT-6, all \extMtRecordsGpt{} documents in one
interleaved run. Noise is now the change between two mines of the same text, and the permutation
effect the change between a permutation and the original from the other repeat. Re-mining is
balanced (\extMtEqNoiseUpGpt{} rises, \extMtEqNoiseDownGpt{} falls beyond $\tau$,
$p=\extMtEqNoisePGpt$), so the earlier drift came from mining in separate runs. Permutation is not:
it moves the score by $\extMtPermMeanGpt$ on average against $\extMtNoiseMeanGpt$ for re-mining, a
difference of $\extMtEqDiffGpt$ with 90\% interval [\extMtEqLoGpt, \extMtEqHiGpt], and upwards
more often than downwards (\extMtEqPermUpGpt{} against \extMtEqPermDownGpt, $p=\extMtEqPermPGpt$).
This comparison is confounded, however. ContraDoc's documents are split into paragraphs at blank
lines, so in its 94 Wikipedia documents every section header (``= = History = ='') is a paragraph and
a claim of its own, and a permutation separates headers from their sections and can move the title
into the middle of the text. Permuted documents are therefore partly degraded, not reordered, and
both the extra movement of $\LCS$ and the judge's falls may reflect the damage rather than order.
A rebuilt set that keeps headers with their sections is needed before the ContraDoc order result
can be read.

\subsection{Further Analyses}
\label{app:ext-further}

These analyses are not needed for the four properties. The first two concern the sign of a
relation when claims are false, the rest how well the miner recovers annotated relations.

\paragraph{The sign follows the truth (ChatProtect).} ChatProtect's \extCpPairs{} pairs give \extCpSweepNGpt{} (relation, world) cases between the two
sentences. In every case the leave-one-out contribution of the relation is negative exactly when
the world falls in the relation's violated cells. This checks the implementation on natural
graphs and confirms Lemma~\ref{lem:edit} at work. With gpt-oss-120b the sweep covers
\extCpSweepNOss{} cases, every one with the predicted sign.

On the subset whose false side the annotators recorded, the contradictions found are
\extCpRealSupportGpt{} supports and \extCpRealConflictGpt{} conflicts at the real verdicts. A
self-contradiction between two false sentences, or between a true and a false one, is a support
at the verdict world. Counting contradictions would treat all of them as defects.


\paragraph{ContraDoc at the verdict world.} With the inserted sentence false and its
contradiction found, $\LCS$ rises on \extCdVerdEdgeIncGpt{} and falls on \extCdVerdEdgeDecGpt{} of
\extCdVerdEdgeNGpt{} pairs ($p=\extCdVerdEdgePGpt$; Table~\ref{tab:ext-contradoc}): the predicted
direction, but not significantly. With the inserted sentence false, the \extCdAssertEdgeNGpt{} graphs with a
found contradiction draw \extCdEvSupGpt{} relations to it, all of them supports and
\extCdEvConGpt{} conflicts. Every one of the \extCdVerdFallsGpt{} pairs whose score nevertheless
fell has no conflict on the inserted sentence: the two versions were mined independently, and
the rest of their graphs came out differently. The sign of each relation follows the truth
values, and the comparison across documents carries the miner's sampling noise. A paired design,
mining the clean document once and adding only the inserted claim's relations, would remove that
noise. With gpt-oss-120b, \extCdEvSupOss{} of the relations drawn to the false sentence
are supports and \extCdEvConOss{} a conflict (an inference drawn from a true claim to the false
one, which the sign rule correctly charges); \extCdVerdFallsNoConOss{} of its \extCdVerdFallsOss{}
verdict-world falls have no conflict on the inserted sentence.

\toprule
& & \multicolumn{2}{c}{GPT-6} & \multicolumn{2}{c}{gpt-oss} \\
\cmidrule(lr){3-4}\cmidrule(l){5-6}

\paragraph{GDTB.} Each item gives the miner one relation's two arguments in their sentences. The
upper block of Table~\ref{tab:ext-gdtb} measures recall of the coupling; the lower block measures
the compile map's central claim, that contrast, concession and temporal sequence constrain
nothing. The difference between the two rates, \extGdCorrectGpt\% against \extGdNoneGpt\%, has a
95\% interval well above zero. The weakest categories are those the miner most often maps to a
neighboring coupling: disjunction and restatement. The \sense{Evidence} category
(PDTB \sense{Cause+Belief}) has no instance in the GDTB documents we use, so it is
absent from the table.

\paragraph{QT30.} Over \extQtWindows{} windows of the BBC debates, the GPT-6 arm reaches
pair-level precision, recall and F1 of \extQtPairPGpt, \extQtPairRGpt{} and \extQtPairFGpt, and a
coupling-level precision, recall and F1 of \extQtCoupPGpt, \extQtCoupRGpt{} and \extQtCoupFGpt.
gpt-oss-120b reaches \extQtPairFOss{} and \extQtCoupFOss, with
inference recall \extQtRecEntailmentOss\%. GPT-6's recall by coupling:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.2em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=2pt]
\item inference: \extQtRecEntailmentGpt\% of \extQtNEntailment, with the direction right in
  \extQtDirGpt\% of those found;
\item rephrase: \extQtRecEquivalenceGpt\% of \extQtNEquivalence; another \extQtEqvAsEnt{} are
  mined as inferences;
\item conflict: \extQtRecContradictionGpt\% of \extQtNContradiction.
\end{itemize}
Inference Anchoring Theory annotates the inferences and conflicts that speakers' moves imply,
including across speakers' turns. Our miners are instructed to emit only relations
the text draws, which caps recall on this corpus by design.
